BXL-2425-00011-v5.headline: Ban gas patio heaters on Brussels café and restaurant terraces from June 2026 — but keep electric terrace heaters allowed.
BXL-2425-00011-v5.proposed_by: Projet d'ordonnance tabled by Minister Alain Maron (Ecolo), government of the Brussels-Capital Region; amendment no. 1 (art. 9) and amendment no. 2 (art. 10) tabled by Pascal Smet (Vooruit.brussels), Aurélie Czekalski, Clémentine Barzin, Gaëtan Van Goidsenhoven, Geoffroy Coomans de Brachène, Loubna Azghoud, Ludivine de Magnanville, Olivier Willocx, Anne-Charlotte d'Ursel, Ilyas Mouani (MR/Vooruit.brussels coalition)
BXL-2425-00011-v5.source_brief:
A Brussels ordinance transposes energy-sobriety rules from the regional Air-Climate-Energy Plan into law: shop doors must be closed, illuminated signs turned off at night, and outdoor heating on commercial terraces banned. At article-by-article discussion, a cross-party amendment stripped the words "de l'électricité ou" from the ban, exempting electric heaters from it indefinitely while the gas-heater ban from June 2026 stood.

- **What the ordinance does:** codifies into law a 2022 royal decree requiring energy-saving behaviour from Brussels businesses — closing entrance doors, shutting off illuminated advertising overnight, and banning all terrace heaters.
- **The flashpoint amendment:** the Fédération Horeca Bruxelles lobbied for electric heaters to be excluded; supporters argue gas combustion produces 40 times more greenhouse gases than nuclear electricity and 490 times more than renewable, making the parallel with electric vehicles coherent.
- **Minister's counter:** Minister Maron warned of a likely equal-treatment legal challenge — electric heaters consume at least as many kWh as gas ones, so banning gas but allowing electric ad vitam aeternam undermines the ordinance's energy-reduction purpose and may be struck down by the Constitutional Court.
- **The rub:** supporters say the amendment protects a struggling horeca sector with negligible climate impact; opponents argue heating open air with electricity is the same ecological absurdity as heating it with gas, and that Paris is the only city to have banned such heaters at all, suggesting the whole provision is largely symbolic.
deep_facts: The text is a projet d'ordonnance modifying various provisions of Brussels energy, climate and waste law; its core aim is to give legal force to energy-sobriety measures first introduced by a 2022 arrêté under the Plan air-climat-énergie, covering illuminated signs, open shop doors and all outdoor terrace heating (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Articles 9 and 10 of the ordinance, as originally drafted, banned 'de l'électricité ou du gaz' for terrace heating on commercial premises; amendments no. 1 and no. 2, tabled by Pascal Smet (Vooruit.brussels) and co-signers from MR, deleted 'de l'électricité ou' from each article, making the ban gas-only with no sunset date for electric (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Amendment mover Smet argued that only one city in the world — Paris — has banned electric heaters, and that even there controls are not strictly enforced and the ban is circumvented; he said the measure was 'purely symbolic' as electric heater consumption is negligible in total Brussels energy use (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

MR speaker Clémentine Barzin cited the Fédération Horeca Bruxelles as having itself requested the amendment, arguing gas combustion produces 40 times more greenhouse gases than nuclear electricity and 490 times more than renewable electricity, and that the analogy with banning fossil-fuel cars while allowing electric ones was correct (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Minister Maron rebutted the car analogy: the LEZ aims to improve air quality by phasing out the most polluting vehicles, whereas this ordinance aims to reduce total energy consumption regardless of source; electric heaters consume at least as many kWh as gas ones, making any ban on gas-only heaters incoherent in energy terms (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Maron also warned of a 'risque juridique évident' — an equal-treatment challenge: how can merchants who invested in gas heaters be required to remove them while those who invested in electric heaters may continue ad vitam aeternam, given both consume the same energy? (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Ecolo speaker Soiresse Njall argued the amendment offered 'no perspective' — electric heaters would remain allowed even after the horeca sector recovered, sending no signal on energy sobriety; heating outdoor air, whether with gas or electricity, is 'une absurdité écologique' (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Groen speaker Stijn Bex, himself a lawyer, questioned whether the gas/electricity distinction had been sufficiently demonstrated to justify different legal treatment, and noted Parliament had already seen one law — the LEZ amendment — fail before the Constitutional Court since the elections (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).
BXL-2425-00011-v5.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The amendment's real logic is economic, not environmental: in a period of coalition formation and with horeca under financial stress, allowing electric heaters hands a business-friendly coalition partner a visible, low-cost win — the climate argument is a post-hoc justification for what is structurally a sector-relief measure.
- Maron's equal-treatment warning is technically credible but strategically useful to the majority: framing a likely Constitutional Court loss as the opponents' problem lets the majority claim it acted in good faith if the provision is later struck, without having to reverse it themselves.
- The 'only Paris did this, and Paris doesn't enforce it' move reframes legislative boldness as naïve exceptionalism, a recurring technique to normalise inaction by pointing to lax enforcement elsewhere rather than to the policy objective.
- The ordinance nonetheless retains its core architecture: gas heaters banned from 2026, shop doors closed, illuminated signs off at night — the electric-heater carve-out is politically visible but energy-marginal, which is precisely why the coalition could afford to grant it.
BXL-2425-00011-v5.raw_fr: Le projet d'ordonnance transpose dans la loi bruxelloise des mesures de sobriete energetique prevues dans le plan air-climat-energie de 2022 : fermeture des portes de commerce, extinction des enseignes lumineuses et interdiction des chauffages de terrasse. Un amendement adopte en seance pleniere a exonere les chaufferettes electriques de l'interdiction, ne maintenant que le ban sur les appareils a gaz a partir de juin 2026. Le ministre Maron a souleve un risque juridique d'inegalite de traitement entre commercants selon le type d'equipement.

BXL-2425-00011-v9.headline: Demand that Brussels social housing puts homeless people higher up the waiting list and expands Housing First, so fewer people sleep on the street.
BXL-2425-00011-v9.proposed_by: Farida Tahar (Ecolo) and Kalvin Soiresse Njall (Ecolo), with original work by former member Pierre-Yves Lux (Ecolo); rapporteurs Martin Casier and Louis de Clippele
BXL-2425-00011-v9.source_brief:
Brussels counts at least 10,000 people sleeping rough or in precarious shelter, against a backdrop of more than 50,000 households on the social-housing waiting list. This resolution, prepared over the previous legislature, asks the Brussels Region to better arm its social-housing operators (SLRB, SISP) to prioritise homeless people, involve communes and CPAS more actively, and hard-wire Housing First logic into allocation policy.

- **What it asks:** that social housing companies (SISP) progressively increase the share of allocations bypassing the waiting list in favour of homeless people, that the Fonds du logement improve access to rental guarantees, and that housing and social-health policy be formally bridged.
- **The contested amendment:** an amendment was tabled drawing on article 11 of Bruss'help's master plan, targeting 33 % of annual SISP allocations (roughly 2,000 units) for homeless people by 2030 — nearly double the current derogation rate; it was rejected.
- **The hesitation in the chamber:** much of the debate turned on procedural and substantive doubts: the base text was seen as outdated (its original version dated from February 2024), several measures had already been implemented by the outgoing government, and critics argued the quota approach risked pitting two groups of poor people against each other in a market already short of supply.
- **The rub:** supporters argue that without a Housing First anchor in allocation law the Brussels homeless count will keep rising; opponents counter that reserving a fixed share of scarce social housing for one vulnerable group, without new supply or clear support budgets, simply organises competition between the poor.
deep_facts: The latest Brussels homeless count (carried out November 2024, figures not yet published at the time of debate) was expected to exceed the approximately 7,000 recorded in the previous official count; multiple speakers cited the figure of at least 10,000 people sleeping rough or in precarious situations (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

More than 50,000 households were on the Brussels social-housing waiting list at the time of debate, with average waiting times exceeding twelve years according to several speakers; N-VA placed the figure at up to 60,000 (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

The outgoing Brussels government had in April 2024 adopted an arrêté raising the minimum quota of social housing allocated to homeless people to 3 % from January 2025, 5 % in 2026, and 6 % in 2027; the resolution was designed to support and reinforce that trajectory (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Ecolo's amendment, drawn from article 11 of the Bruss'help master plan, sought a target of 33 % of annual SISP allocations for homeless people by 2030, equating to roughly 738 of the 2,214 social housing units allocated per year; opponents noted that of those 2,214 annual allocations, only about 1,000 actually become free for waiting-list families — the rest going to internal rotations and existing derogations (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

A ULB applied-economics study cited in debate concluded that accompanying homeless people into durable rehousing is economically more efficient than maintaining emergency-shelter systems; this was cited as the academic foundation for the Housing First approach in the resolution (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Glasgow was cited by Ecolo as having instituted an 80 % social-housing allocation quota for homeless people despite having a lower social-housing stock than Brussels, as evidence that ambitious quotas are operationally feasible (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

PS speaker El Yousfi objected that the resolution was 'almost identical' to a text tabled by former member Pierre-Yves Lux in February 2024 without updating it for regulatory changes that had since taken place, including the April 2024 arrêté; she called the text 'depassé' (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Les Engagés noted that several measures in the resolution had already been enacted, others had been rejected by the sector, and the remainder would require budgets for the next government to allocate; the group's abstention was 'not a rejection of principle but an exigency of method and efficiency' (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

DéFI cited the SLRB's own managing director as having warned of 'situations explosives' from placing a particularly vulnerable population into housing structures already occupied by people in precarious situations, without guaranteed support resources (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).

Vlaams Belang tabled two amendments to the resolution: one limiting social-housing access to holders of a legal residence permit, and one requiring SLRB and SISP to systematically check whether tenants held undeclared property abroad; both were rejected almost across the board (CRI, 31 Jan 2025).
BXL-2425-00011-v9.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The near-universal abstention on the base text is not indifference: it reflects a peculiar Brussels alignment where even groups sympathetic to the goal — PS, PTB, Les Engagés — declined to hand opposition Ecolo a legislative win before a new government is formed, particularly on a text they regard as stale and partly superseded.
- The 33 % quota amendment is the resolution's only genuinely new operative element; its rejection is therefore the real political event — it signals that a cross-partisan majority is unwilling to bind the incoming government to an allocation formula that could generate court challenges from waiting-list families displaced by it.
- The 'competition between the poor' framing, deployed by Team Fouad Ahidar, PTB and others from very different political traditions, converges to protect the status quo against a supply-side critique: if everyone agrees the root cause is too few units, a quota debate becomes a diversion unless paired with a construction plan, which the resolution does not include.
- Ecolo's explicit framing of the resolution as 'a signal to our successors' rather than an executable programme reveals the text's true register: it is politics-of-record, staking out a position for coalition negotiations rather than legislating — which is precisely why most groups felt comfortable abstaining rather than voting yes or no.
BXL-2425-00011-v9.raw_fr: La proposition de resolution demande a la Region bruxelloise de mobiliser les societes de logement social (SISP, SLRB) et les agences immobilieres sociales en faveur des personnes sans abri, d'ameliorer l'acces aux garanties locatives via le Fonds du logement et de mieux articuler les politiques du logement et celles du social-sante. Un amendement visant a porter progressivement a 33 % d'ici 2030 la part des attributions reservees aux sans-abri, inspire du plan directeur de Bruss'help, a ete rejete.
